% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{The problem}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}
    \item Critical software is produced faster than people can review it: AI writes it, agents run it, AI-assisted auditing finds every flaw.
    \item Assurance today is a chain of trusted components: developer, reviewer, compiler, analysis tools, runtime. Each is a single point of failure.
    \item Memory-safe languages trust the compiler. Sandboxes see untyped bytes. Verifiers say nothing about bugs in compiler or runtime.
  \end{itemize}
  \takeaway{How to run code nobody fully trusts, with guarantees that survive a bug in any one component?}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{The product: Verex}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
        \item Teams write ordinary Rust; Verex verifies and runs it.
        \item Any language with ownership and borrowing; Move, the origin, included.
        \item Proofs before deployment, independent checks during execution.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \textbf{What owners get}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\small
        \item Mathematical proofs, not only tests
        \item Independent redundancy of the checks
        \item Containment of untrusted code
        \item Defined failure instead of silent corruption
        \item Reproducible execution, bit for bit
        \item Bounded, metered resources
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \takeaway{Run code you do not trust, and know what it can and cannot do.}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Design principle: no single trusted component}
  \begingroup\centering
  \begin{tikzpicture}[font=\scriptsize, x=1cm, y=1cm,
      stage/.style={proc, minimum width=2.3cm, minimum height=8mm}]
    \node[art, draw=black!60, minimum width=2.0cm, minimum height=8mm] (src) at (0,0) {Source\\Move or Rust};
    \node[ext, minimum width=2.0cm, minimum height=8mm] (cc) at (2.7,0) {Compiler\\\emph{untrusted}};
    \node[stage] (bv) at (5.6,0) {Bytecode verifier\\at load time};
    \node[stage] (rc) at (8.5,0) {Runtime checks\\during execution};
    \node[stage] (vm) at (11.4,0) {MonoVM\\deterministic, metered};
    \node[stage] (pv) at (2.7,1.3) {Prover\\before deployment};
    \draw[arr] (src) -- (cc);
    \draw[arr] (cc) -- (bv);
    \draw[arr] (bv) -- (rc);
    \draw[arr] (rc) -- (vm);
    \draw[arr] (src.north) |- (pv.west);
    \draw[feed] (pv.east) -| node[pos=0.25, lbl] {proved properties} (vm.north);
  \end{tikzpicture}
  \par\endgroup
  \medskip
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
    \item Every safety invariant (typing, resources, references, memory) is established at least twice, by independent implementations.
    \item The bytecode verifier trusts nothing from the compiler; the runtime checks trust nothing from the verifier.
    \item Possible because the type system makes safety checkable on bytecode, and references never alias.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Supply chain attacks and deployment modes}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \textbf{Injected code}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
        \item Arrives through the tools the platform does not trust.
        \item Cannot forge an authorization token, duplicate an asset, or reach a value it holds no reference to.
        \item Type and resource safety bound the damage.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \textbf{Two deployment modes}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
        \item \textbf{MonoVM}: all layers in place.
        \item \textbf{Native}: for real-time loops and numeric kernels; proofs hold, the native compiler is trusted.
        \item MonoVM stays for simulation, differential testing and shadow execution.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{The platform today}
  Implemented and open source in the Aptos code base; years of production with billions of dollars at stake.
  \medskip
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
    \item \textbf{Move}: Rust-like types, first-class functions, linear resources, borrow discipline.
    \item \textbf{Move Prover}: contracts and invariants, SMT and Lean, fast enough for CI.
    \item \textbf{Bytecode verifier}: typing, abilities and references at load time.
    \item \textbf{Runtime safety checks}: the same, with separate code; stopped real exploits that passed the verifier.
    \item \textbf{MonoVM}: monomorphized code, flat values, 30--50$\times$ faster; validated by mainnet replay.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}[fragile]{Extending the platform to Rust}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \textbf{Why it fits}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
        \item Sequential safe Rust and Move enforce the same aliasing rule.
        \item So Rust compiles to bytecode whose safety stays checkable; Wasm and native code discard it.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \textbf{The subset}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
        \item Sequential and deterministic, including floating point.
        \item Recursive types, interior mutability and raw pointers included.
        \item Everything else is rejected with a diagnostic.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \medskip
  \textbf{Four bytecode extensions}, from borrow-checked MIR
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\small
    \item References inside structs: lifetime parameters, checked by the verifier.
    \item Recursive types through |Box| and |Rc|, heap objects in MonoVM.
    \item Interior mutability: native cells with dynamic borrow state.
    \item Raw pointers with checked semantics.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}[fragile]{Unsafe code under a checked memory model}
  Native Rust: raw-pointer misuse is undefined behavior. Verex: every raw-pointer operation is checked.
  \medskip
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
        \item Strict provenance, allocation identities never reused, typed allocations.
        \item Use after free, double free, out of bounds, invalid reinterpretation: a located abort.
        \item Raw pointer to reference is a dynamic reborrow, checked like any reference.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
        \item The prover discharges the same conditions; where no check can fail, the VM skips it.
        \item Purpose: reuse existing Rust crates without rewriting them.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Verification for Rust and numeric code}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}
    \item \textbf{Automated}: the Move Prover's methods carry over, since they rest on the shared reference discipline; SMT in CI.
    \item \textbf{Kernel-checked}: the Lean-based verifier proves a contract as a theorem about the program's semantics; absence of undefined behavior included.
    \item \textbf{Specification inference}: abort and postconditions inferred mechanically, invariants and intent with AI. People review specifications instead of writing them.
    \item \textbf{Numeric code}: specified over the reals with error bounds; deterministic floating point makes results reproducible.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Evidence to date}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}
    \item Prover in CI on the Aptos framework: block prologue, staking, metering, code deployment.
    \item Runtime checks stopped proof-of-concept exploits that passed the static verifier.
    \item Reference checker replayed billions of transactions without a false alarm.
    \item Runtime check cost: about 10\% for types and abilities; 26--29\% for references, before optimization.
    \item MonoVM: 30--50$\times$ the current Move VM on recorded blocks.
  \end{itemize}
  \medskip
  Comparisons with WebAssembly runtimes and native Rust are in preparation.
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Application domains}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{3pt}
    \item \textbf{Agent-generated code}: metered, isolated, replayable, with inferred and proved properties.
    \item \textbf{Financial logic}: settlement, clearing, risk limits, pricing; resources model assets, invariants express conservation.
    \item \textbf{Safety-critical and defense}: proved control laws, bounded resources, reproducible numerics.
    \item \textbf{Multi-party computation}: run a partner's or regulator's code without trusting their toolchain.
    \item \textbf{Existing Rust}: plugins and libraries with unsafe internals, hardened without rewriting.
  \end{itemize}
  \takeaway{Adoption starts with one component where failure is most expensive, run next to the existing system.}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Relation to existing approaches}
  \small
  \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}P{0.34\textwidth}cccc@{}}
    & \textbf{Proves} & \textbf{Checks at load} & \textbf{Runtime checks} & \textbf{Deterministic} \\
    \hline
    \textbf{Verex} & \yes & \yes & \yes & \yes \\
    Wasm runtimes & \no & \partly & \partly & \partly \\
    JVM, CLR & \no & \yes & \partly & \no \\
    Rust verifiers (Verus, Kani, \ldots) & \yes & \no & \no & \no \\
    SPARK / Ada & \yes & \no & \partly & \no \\
    K framework & \yes & \no & \partly & \partly \\
    Miri & \no & \no & \partly & \no \\
    zkVMs & \no & \no & \no & \yes \\
  \end{tabular}
  \par\medskip
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}
    \item zkVMs prove that code ran, not that it is correct; complementary.
    \item Specialized, not generic: every layer relies on the ownership discipline.
  \end{itemize}
  \par
  {\footnotesize \yes\ yes\quad \partly\ partial, e.g.\ memory bounds only, or left to the embedder\quad \no\ no}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Roadmap}
  \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}P{0.16\textwidth}P{0.78\textwidth}@{}}
    \textbf{0--4 months} & Rust Stage 0 pipeline; deterministic floating point; checked raw pointers in the Lean verifier; MonoVM standalone; benchmarks against Wasm and native; first design partners \\
    \textbf{4--8 months} & Lifetime-annotated bytecode and recursive types; checked raw pointers in the VM; prover for the Rust subset; production reference checker; specification inference as a product \\
    \textbf{8--14 months} & Lifetime-checked verifier for untrusted Rust bytecode; verified library models; compiler correctness for core fragments; ahead-of-time compilation; tool qualification groundwork \\
  \end{tabular}
  \par\medskip
  {\small Assumes sufficient staffing.}
\end{frame}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{frame}{Open problems}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}
    \item \textbf{Sound lifetime checking of adversarial bytecode}: a new verifier algorithm is needed.
    \item \textbf{Ecosystem coverage}: how much real Rust fits the subset.
    \item \textbf{Fidelity for unsafe code}: no normative Rust memory model exists.
    \item \textbf{Performance against native}: JIT or AOT from verified bytecode that keeps the runtime checks.
    \item \textbf{Specification effort}: loop invariants and numeric error bounds remain hardest.
    \item \textbf{Certification}: tool qualification and long-term support.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}
